title: Texting Old Cleaning Leads: The 14.6% Opt-Out Day and What Fixed It
description: What happened when we texted about 1,500 old cleaning-company leads: a day-one account lock, the real cause, and the order to do it in so it doesn't happen to you.
author: Roy Banwell
content:
A residential cleaning company I built a lead follow-up system for had about 1,500 old leads sitting in a Google Sheet. Some went back to September 2024. Nobody had ever followed up with them. The plan was simple: text them, get some back. On the first day of sending, the account got locked. Here is what happened, why, and the order I would do it in now.

The short answer

Split the old list by how old each lead is, and text only the freshest group first. Check every lead source against your current customers before anything goes out. Register your number for business texting. Watch your opt-out rate on day one. Slowing down the pace does not fix a bad list, because the platform's limit is a percentage, not a volume.

What went wrong on day one

The first day of live sends went to 48 people. Seven replied STOP. That is a 14.6% opt-out rate.

The texting provider behind GoHighLevel documents its limit at 3% opt-outs. Cross it and the whole account's texting is locked for 24 hours, automatically. It is a routine compliance gate, not a carrier blacklist, but it means every text the business sends stops for a day, including replies to new leads.

The cause was the list, not the speed. Someone who asked for a quote 15 months ago and never heard back does not remember you. A fair share of them will text STOP. The pace was cut to 3 texts an hour, 10am to 6pm, but that does not change the percentage. A slow trickle to a stale list still opts out at a stale-list rate.

The fix: split the list by age

We sorted the whole reactivation list (about 1,540 people across website and Facebook leads) by the date each lead first came in:

Lead agePeople
0 to 3 months628
3 to 6 months226
6 to 12 months446
12+ months154
Unknown date84

Only the 0 to 3 month group was queued for texting. The older groups were held back. The 34 people who had already received the first text were taken out so nobody got it twice. The freshest three months of a list behave completely differently from the 12+ month tail, and that is the single most useful thing I learned on this build.

The second mistake: texting current customers

Old lead lists always contain people who booked later and are happy clients today. Texting them "it's been a while!" makes you look like you do not know your own customers.

We had a filter that removed anyone who booked in the last 45 days, but it was only applied to the Facebook leads. The website leads went in without it. When we ran the same check on them afterward, it caught 88 current customers, and at least one had already received the text. Run the customer check on every source before the first send.

The parts that worked

  • Clean the phone numbers. Checking numbers against real North American numbering rules, not just a digit count, found 12 bad numbers out of 1,246 (about 1%). Those contacts still had valid emails, so they got email instead of being dropped.
  • Register your number. Business texting at volume in the US requires A2P 10DLC registration with the carriers. Nothing was sent until it was approved.
  • Send from a person. Texts came from the owner's name at a dedicated number, not a no-reply system.
  • Keep it short. A friendly reintro text, then one follow-up four days later with a $30 offer, then a long, gentle nurture over roughly 140 days.
  • Ask for a reply, not a click. A cleaning quote needs a conversation (home size, condition, pets), so the texts ask a question instead of pushing a booking link.
  • Stop the moment someone books. A booking from the scheduling software tags the contact and removes them from every sequence, so nobody who just booked gets a "still interested?" text.

The order I would do it in now

  1. Import every lead into one CRM with a tag for its source.
  2. Remove current customers from every source, not just one.
  3. Validate phone numbers and register the texting number.
  4. Split by lead age. Start with the last 3 months only.
  5. Send slowly, and check the opt-out rate at the end of day one. Under 3% is the line.
  6. Only then try the 3 to 12 month groups. For anything older than a year, use email or leave it alone.

This post is about the mistakes, not a results claim. I will update it with booking numbers from the old-list sends once they exist.

Frequently Asked Questions

What opt-out rate gets a texting account locked?

On GoHighLevel's texting provider, the documented threshold is 3%. Cross it and texting for the whole account is locked for 24 hours. Our first day of texting old leads hit 14.6%.

Should I text leads that are more than a year old?

Be careful. They are the most likely to opt out, and a high opt-out rate can lock your account for everyone, including new leads. Start with your freshest leads and treat the 12+ month group as email-only or skip it.

Will sending more slowly prevent opt-outs?

No. A slower pace keeps the volume manageable, but the account limit is a percentage. If the list is stale, a slow trickle opts out at the same rate.

Do I need special registration to text leads?

In the US, yes. Business texting from a regular number requires A2P 10DLC registration with the carriers. Without it, many messages are filtered or blocked.

How do I avoid texting my current customers?

Before the first send, compare every lead source against a recent export of your bookings (we used the last 45 days) and remove the matches. Do it for every source, not just the one you checked first.
